title: Steve Eisman Reflects on 2008, The Big Short & Today’s K-Shaped Economy | The Real Eisman Playbook
summary: At a university Q&A recorded October 29 and published December 1, 2025, Eisman explains the financial crisis through leverage, bad underwriting, concentrated ownership and interconnected derivatives. He favors US equities and continued AI spending, expects bank consolidation, and explicitly withholds an opinion on private-credit insurance risk. The historical credit framework is useful; several absolute claims about regulation, investigations and financing need qualification.
assessment: The strongest material explanation is the interaction of credit deterioration, leverage and funding. His stated uncertainty on private credit is preserved rather than rewritten as a bearish forecast. Regulatory and due-diligence simplifications are weaker, and an optimistic AI-spending scenario is not an unconditional market target.
framework_points: Study the debt and funding structure behind equity narratives.
Look for a shared hidden assumption, such as permanently rising house prices.
Refresh conviction with recurring operating or loan-vintage data.
Choose an instrument whose carrying cost lets the thesis survive.
Say when the available data do not support an opinion.
Distinguish a sound business or technology from a good investment at the prevailing price.
tools_and_charts: Bank stress tests and capital ratios
Capex guidance and corporate cash flow
Visa spending and bank credit-quality results
transcript_cautions: The introduction dates the event October 29, 2025, although this video was published December 1. Statements about current conditions refer to the recording.
Captions garble company names including Comerica and New Century; obvious names were corrected from context.
The risk-weighted leverage and mortgage examples are simplified, not calibrated models.
Opening montage repeats later passages; ads, personal biography, movie anecdotes and career advice are excluded from material-claim counts.
speaker_map_notes: Eisman is the main respondent. Ivy Zelman hosts; students ask questions. Student premises are not assigned to Eisman unless he explicitly adopts them.

claims.claim: Gross leverage at major financial institutions tripled between 1997 and 2007 while risk-weighted leverage stayed flat.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: The precise universe, balance-sheet definition and endpoints are unspecified. Primary data show substantial variation across firms; the blanket multiple is not established.

evidence.finding: The 2000-2007 ratios varied sharply by bank, including roughly stable ratios at JPMorgan and Wells Fargo. Reported versus off-balance-sheet leverage also differed. This does not establish a uniform tripling from 1997.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

assumptions: A bilateral protection contract without a fully effective independent guarantee.
proof.derivation: The promised payment is valuable only to the extent the protection seller or pledged collateral can satisfy it.

claims.claim: Tax refunds seasonally improve borrower payment capacity, so temporary spring credit improvement can mislead an analyst.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use monthly vintage delinquency data and seasonal adjustments around refund receipts.
claims.reason: A testable seasonal mechanism is proposed, but the specific historical price-rally attribution and size of the effect are not independently verified.
claims.next_check: Use monthly vintage delinquency data and seasonal adjustments around refund receipts.

claims.claim: The growth of private credit and insurer ownership is insufficient evidence by itself to conclude that a crisis is coming.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Look for asset, liability, leverage and loss data before forming a crisis forecast.
claims.reason: This is an explicit limit on his knowledge and a research standard, not a prediction of safety or failure.
claims.next_check: Look for asset, liability, leverage and loss data before forming a crisis forecast.

claims.claim: Post-crisis regulation and stress testing materially increased bank resilience by increasing capital and reducing risky exposures.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare consistent bank capital, leverage and risk measures before and after reform.
claims.reason: The Fed confirms a substantial post-crisis capital increase. Exact claims about leverage being more than halved everywhere are not independently resolved.

evidence.title: 2025 stress test background
evidence.finding: Large-bank capital rose substantially after the crisis. Stress testing applies on annual or two-year cycles to covered firms, not uniformly to every bank.

claims.next_check: Compare consistent bank capital, leverage and risk measures before and after reform.

claims.claim: US banks are basically safe under the post-crisis framework.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define the bank population, loss threshold, scenario and horizon before scoring safety.
claims.reason: He immediately discusses SVB as an exception. Neither a universal safety guarantee nor a precise horizon is stated.
claims.next_check: Define the bank population, loss threshold, scenario and horizon before scoring safety.

claims.claim: SVB essentially just took venture deposits and bought long-term Treasuries; that was its business.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare the year-end 2022 loan and securities balance sheet, including agency mortgage-backed securities.
claims.reason: The description is materially oversimplified. An inspected supervisory account establishes securities and interest-rate exposure, but this review has not yet attached the full asset table needed for a definitive composition grade.

evidence.title: Review of SVB supervision: key takeaways
evidence.finding: Concentrated uninsured deposits, interest-rate risk and weak liquidity management left SVB vulnerable; the securities sale and proposed capital raise preceded a run exceeding $40 billion on March 9.

claims.next_check: Compare the year-end 2022 loan and securities balance sheet, including agency mortgage-backed securities.

claims.claim: SVB failed when interest-rate losses interacted with concentrated deposit withdrawals and the need to monetize assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Trace securities losses, liquid resources and deposit outflows.
claims.reason: The Fed review documents this funding and duration interaction. It also identifies governance and risk-management weaknesses.

claims.claim: Large public growth-stock losses imply comparable percentage losses in the private businesses held by venture capital.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Match public and private cash flows, financing terms and valuations before transferring a drawdown.
claims.reason: Public repricing is relevant evidence, but identical percentage changes require matching businesses, terms and starting valuations. No such comparison is supplied.
claims.next_check: Match public and private cash flows, financing terms and valuations before transferring a drawdown.

claims.claim: There are essentially no newly underwritten subprime mortgages in the United States.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define subprime and compare current originations in that category rather than conflating borrower scores with loan structures.
claims.reason: He softens the literal zero, but does not define subprime as borrower credit quality, product structure or private securitization. Modern low-score government-insured loans are not equivalent to pre-crisis subprime products.
claims.next_check: Define subprime and compare current originations in that category rather than conflating borrower scores with loan structures.

claims.claim: He knows of no mortgage-underwriting regulation; the real constraint is the bank stress test.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect applicable underwriting rules and the population subject to stress tests.
claims.qualifications: He qualifies the first clause as his knowledge, but presents it as the explanation of the regulatory constraint.
claims.reason: Covered mortgage lenders have an explicit ability-to-repay duty under Regulation Z. Stress tests are important but cannot substitute for this underwriting regime.

evidence.title: Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage final rule
evidence.finding: Covered mortgage creditors must make a reasonable, good-faith ability-to-repay determination. Mortgage underwriting rules exist independently of bank stress tests.

evidence.title: 2025 stress test background
evidence.finding: Large-bank capital rose substantially after the crisis. Stress testing applies on annual or two-year cycles to covered firms, not uniformly to every bank.

claims.next_check: Inspect applicable underwriting rules and the population subject to stress tests.

claims.claim: Technology and compliance costs favor scale, and regional-bank consolidation should accelerate.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Track announced and completed regional-bank deals, asset concentration and unit-cost changes against a specified baseline.
claims.reason: A major cited deal subsequently closed. That supports consolidation activity, while one transaction does not prove an industry-wide wave or its causal explanation.

evidence.title: Fifth Third completes Comerica merger
evidence.finding: The announced merger closed, creating a bank with about $294 billion in assets. One transaction supports consolidation activity but does not establish an industry-wide wave or the causal necessity of scale.

claims.next_check: Track announced and completed regional-bank deals, asset concentration and unit-cost changes against a specified baseline.

claims.claim: The Fed is institutionally stronger than alarmist coverage suggests, and the next chair will not pursue uncontrolled easing.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify a policy-rate path and an operational independence test.
claims.reason: No threshold for uncontrolled easing or specific policy path is given. This institutional judgment cannot be scored from a single rate decision.
claims.next_check: Specify a policy-rate path and an operational independence test.

claims.claim: Recurring loan-vintage data can sustain conviction when market prices and consensus disagree.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check whether new data actually test and potentially falsify the thesis.
claims.reason: This is a research practice, not a forecast or a guarantee that conviction is justified.
claims.next_check: Check whether new data actually test and potentially falsify the thesis.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare lending standards, expected losses and later vintage performance.
claims.qualifications: His categorical rejection of any political role is not established by this mechanism alone.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents weak underwriting and incentives within the mortgage boom. This feedback explanation is supported without accepting that policy had no role at all.

evidence.finding: The report documents leverage, deteriorating mortgage underwriting, retained securitization exposure and derivatives counterparty connections. Chapters 8-10 distinguish these mechanisms from a simple housing-price narrative.

claims.speaker: Ivy Zelman
claims.test: Read the original speech and compare lending changes with a defensible causal design.
claims.reason: Zelman offers a causal attribution, but the episode does not establish the incremental effect of that advice versus incentives and other policy conditions.
claims.next_check: Read the original speech and compare lending changes with a defensible causal design.

claims.claim: A debt tranche can express the same bearish thesis with much lower carrying cost than shorting an expensive, high-dividend stock.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare premium, dividend liability, borrow fee, recovery exposure and counterparty risk for the actual trades.
claims.reason: The instrument-selection principle is useful; his personal historical borrow costs are recollections rather than independently verified return records.
claims.next_check: Compare premium, dividend liability, borrow fee, recovery exposure and counterparty risk for the actual trades.

claims.claim: In the simplified waterfall, three 3% layers are exhausted when cumulative pool losses reach 9%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Apply loss allocation to the stated example.
claims.reason: The arithmetic is correct under the stated sequential-loss structure; real transactions also involve cash flows, triggers and recoveries.
claims.next_check: Apply loss allocation to the stated example.

assumptions: Three successive loss-absorbing layers of 3% each; no offsetting recoveries or excess spread.
proof.derivation: 3% + 3% + 3% = 9%; the third layer is fully impaired at that cumulative loss.

claims.claim: Due-diligence samples revealed deficient mortgages, yet securitizations proceeded with inadequate disclosure of loan quality.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare Clayton results, waivers and investor disclosures.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents sampled failures, waivers and disclosure problems. The account should not be read as proof that every firm followed an identical sample size and procedure.

evidence.title: FCIC report, Clayton due diligence findings, printed pp.165-169
evidence.finding: Clayton rejected 28% of sampled loans; banks waived in 39% of those rejected. Samples and disclosure practices varied; the findings support a serious due-diligence failure but not every universal statement about every firm.

claims.next_check: Compare Clayton results, waivers and investor disclosures.

claims.claim: As far as anyone knows, DOJ never even investigated the mortgage due-diligence conduct referred after the crisis inquiry.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate the specific referral, criminal prosecution, civil investigation and settlement outcomes.
claims.reason: DOJ documents investigations and civil resolutions concerning RMBS misconduct. That contradicts a broad impression of no investigation, but does not establish the disposition of every particular FCIC criminal referral.

evidence.title: Goldman Sachs RMBS settlement and admitted facts
evidence.finding: DOJ describes investigations of mortgage securitization misconduct and a $5.06 billion civil resolution. It distinguishes civil liability from criminal charges, which the settlement did not release.

claims.next_check: Separate the specific referral, criminal prosecution, civil investigation and settlement outcomes.

claims.claim: Without bailouts, the crisis would have produced a depression with unemployment near 30%.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use an explicit macro-financial counterfactual model with uncertainty bounds.
claims.reason: The claim is a counterfactual numerical forecast. Neither the observed 2009 recession nor the existence of systemic danger identifies that precise alternative outcome.
claims.next_check: Use an explicit macro-financial counterfactual model with uncertainty bounds.

claims.claim: For-profit education had a structurally poor product sustained by government funding.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare completion, earnings, repayment and public subsidy across named schools and matched alternatives.
claims.reason: This is a broad industry thesis without a defined cohort, outcome measure or new supporting evidence in the episode.
claims.next_check: Compare completion, earnings, repayment and public subsidy across named schools and matched alternatives.

claims.claim: US economic dynamism makes US equities the preferred destination, with little reason to invest abroad.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Specify investable portfolios, currency treatment, starting valuation and horizon.
claims.reason: This preference has no portfolio, benchmark, horizon or valuation constraint. Market-cap leadership alone does not establish future relative returns.
claims.next_check: Specify investable portfolios, currency treatment, starting valuation and horizon.

claims.claim: The economy is increasingly dependent on AI while housing and other segments are weak, and ultimate AI returns remain uncertain.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate direct investment contributions from imports and indirect effects; measure sector breadth and realized cash returns.
claims.reason: The direction is a material diagnostic, but the episode does not provide a reproducible decomposition of AI-attributable GDP or a return calculation.
claims.next_check: Separate direct investment contributions from imports and indirect effects; measure sector breadth and realized cash returns.

claims.claim: AI-investment returns may not be clear until 2027; continued capex expansion keeps the current market story alive.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Revisit realized utilization, revenue, capex and free cash flow through 2027.
claims.reason: The explicit 2027 assessment window is unfinished. Alphabet guidance supports continuing investment at the recording date, but not the eventual return on that spending.

evidence.title: Alphabet Q3 2025 earnings call
evidence.finding: Alphabet raised 2025 capex guidance from $85 billion to $91-93 billion and expected a significant further increase in 2026. Management also identified depreciation and energy-cost pressure.

claims.next_check: Revisit realized utilization, revenue, capex and free cash flow through 2027.

claims.claim: Visa spending and healthy reported bank credit quality argue against an imminent broad consumer collapse.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Combine real spending, payment volume, cohort delinquency and labor income; define the forecast horizon.
claims.reason: The inference is material, but aggregate transaction growth and bank portfolios may conceal weakness by income cohort. The episode does not specify an imminent-collapse threshold.
claims.next_check: Combine real spending, payment volume, cohort delinquency and labor income; define the forecast horizon.

claims.claim: The market should keep rising while hyperscalers expand capex; a major capex cut would trigger a large correction.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.horizon: While the AI capex cycle continues; no fixed end date
claims.test: Track comparable capex guidance and market returns around a material spending reversal.
claims.qualifications: The Meta 25% cut is a hypothetical trigger, not a forecast that Meta will announce it.
claims.reason: This is a conditional market scenario without a fixed terminal date. The capex-cut trigger and ensuing return window require definition before resolution.
claims.next_check: Track comparable capex guidance and market returns around a material spending reversal.

claims.claim: Unlike the internet bubble, the current AI buildout is financed from large profitable companies own cash flows rather than leverage.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile operating cash flow, capex, distributions, new debt and project financing at the recording date.
claims.reason: Profitable incumbents are an important difference, but the categorical financing claim needs full cash-flow, debt and off-balance-sheet evidence across the named firms. Alphabet capex guidance alone cannot resolve it.

evidence.title: Alphabet Q3 2025 earnings call
evidence.finding: Alphabet raised 2025 capex guidance from $85 billion to $91-93 billion and expected a significant further increase in 2026. Management also identified depreciation and energy-cost pressure.

claims.next_check: Reconcile operating cash flow, capex, distributions, new debt and project financing at the recording date.

claims.claim: Housing is no longer an attractive investment beyond roughly keeping pace with inflation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Define a property cohort, net total return and holding period.
claims.qualifications: Eisman rejects the investment framing; Zelman supplies the inflation benchmark.
claims.reason: No location, leverage, rent benefit, holding period or maintenance assumption is specified. A blanket investment outcome is not measurable as stated.
claims.next_check: Define a property cohort, net total return and holding period.

claims.claim: He has bought a small amount of crypto despite his longstanding doubts about its rationale.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use only as a disclosed change in exposure unless verified transaction records are supplied.
claims.reason: This is a personal position disclosure, not evidence of a trade price, realized return or unconditional bullish forecast.
claims.next_check: Use only as a disclosed change in exposure unless verified transaction records are supplied.

claims.claim: Crypto often trades like risky technology equities rather than reliably hedging the inflation and fiat-debasement risks used to justify ownership.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Calculate dated rolling correlations and stress-period returns; distinguish inflation shocks from monetary debasement.
claims.reason: A meaningful hedge test must specify regime, asset and horizon. The episode supplies no current correlation calculation, and a long-run debasement thesis does not imply an inverse relationship on every daily move.
claims.next_check: Calculate dated rolling correlations and stress-period returns; distinguish inflation shocks from monetary debasement.
